title: SC Stays Arbitral Award Signed a Day After Arbitrator's Warrant as Calcutta HC Judge Was Notified
meta_description: Supreme Court stays an award published hours after the arbitrator's warrant as a Calcutta HC judge was notified, and issues notice on its validity.
court: Supreme Court of India (on appeal from the Calcutta High Court)
bench: Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu
case_name: Acumen (J) Marketing Private Limited v. Respondent not named in available reports
citation: SLP arising from AP-COM No. 607/2026 (Calcutta High Court)
body: An arbitral award signed within hours of its author being told he was about to become a High Court judge is now on hold while the Supreme Court works out whether it should have been signed at all. The Court stayed the award on 30 October 2026 and issued notice on a plea by Acumen (J) Marketing Private Limited challenging the Calcutta High Court judgment that let the award stand.

The sequence of events is what makes the case unusual. Sole arbitrator Partha Pratim Roy's mandate in the reference was due to expire on 27 July 2026. The President's warrant appointing him an Additional Judge of the Calcutta High Court was notified on 7 August 2026. The very next day, 8 August 2026, he published the arbitral award, reportedly at around 2 PM. Acumen objected to the Calcutta High Court that an arbitrator could not sign a binding award after formally becoming a sitting or about-to-sit judge, and separately questioned whether his mandate, due to have lapsed in July, had even validly continued through to August.

That objection did not persuade the Calcutta High Court. By its judgment of 12 August 2026 in AP-COM No. 607/2026, it rejected Acumen's objection to the arbitrator's competence and allowed the award to stand, treating the extension of his mandate and the subsequent award as valid despite the timing. Acumen then moved the Supreme Court by special leave petition.

A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu took a different preliminary view. On 30 October 2026, the bench issued notice, made it returnable on 28 November 2026, and stayed the operation of the arbitral award dated 8 August 2026 until the next hearing. One report describes the bench as having called the award prima facie void, a characterisation made at the notice stage and not a final ruling on validity; the question of whether an award signed after the President's warrant of judicial appointment was notified can stand at all remains open for the Court to decide when the matter is heard on 28 November 2026.

Why the timing matters so much becomes clear once the status of an arbitrator mid-transition is examined closely. Once a warrant of appointment as a judge has been notified, the person named in it is, for most practical purposes, no longer available to continue functioning as an ordinary private adjudicator chosen by the parties to an arbitration agreement. Whether that unavailability takes effect the instant the warrant is notified, or only once the person is formally sworn in and takes the oath of office, is exactly the gap this case falls into, since Roy signed the award in the interval between those two points.

Acumen's challenge, read closely, raises two separate objections rather than one. The first is procedural: that an arbitrator cannot continue acting, let alone sign a final award, once his appointment to judicial office has been notified, regardless of whether his arbitral mandate had technically expired earlier. The second goes to the mandate itself: that Roy's authority to act as arbitrator had already lapsed on 27 July 2026, well before the warrant was even notified, so that everything done afterward, the extension as well as the award, rests on an authority that no longer existed. The Supreme Court's stay preserves both arguments for the hearing in November, without indicating which, if either, it finds more persuasive at this stage.

The dispute sits at the intersection of two bodies of law that rarely cross paths: the rules governing when an arbitrator's mandate under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act lapses or gets extended, and the conventions surrounding a sitting arbitrator's transition into judicial office. An arbitrator whose warrant of appointment as a judge has already been notified occupies an uncertain position, no longer purely a private adjudicator chosen by the parties, yet not quite a sitting judge either, and the Supreme Court will have to decide which status governed his authority to sign the award the next day.

Until the Supreme Court decides the point, parties and counsel with pending references where an arbitrator is known to be in line for judicial appointment have a clear practical lesson from this case: get the award signed and published well before any warrant of appointment is notified, or risk the entire award being challenged on exactly the ground Acumen has raised. The stay means the award, whatever its merits, carries no binding effect on either party until the Supreme Court rules on its validity.
why_it_matters: The case sets up a Supreme Court ruling on what happens to an arbitral award signed after the arbitrator's own appointment as a judge has been notified but before he formally takes judicial office. Parties with references pending before an arbitrator who may be elevated to the bench should treat the timing of signing and publishing an award as a real risk factor, not a formality, until the Court settles the point on 28 November 2026 or thereafter.
card_summary: Supreme Court stays an arbitral award that arbitrator Partha Pratim Roy signed a day after his warrant of appointment as a Calcutta High Court judge was notified, issuing notice on Acumen (J) Marketing's challenge.
card_tip: If your arbitrator is reported to be in line for judicial appointment, press for the award to be signed and published before any warrant is notified, to avoid this exact challenge.
verification_notes: The stay order dated 30 October 2026, the bench (Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu), the notice returnable 28 November 2026, the petitioner's identity (Acumen (J) Marketing Private Limited), the underlying Calcutta High Court judgment dated 12 August 2026 in AP-COM No. 607/2026, the arbitrator's name (Partha Pratim Roy), the mandate expiry of 27 July 2026, the warrant notification of 7 August 2026, and the award publication on 8 August 2026 are corroborated across LiveLaw and LawChakra. The characterisation of the award as 'prima facie void' at the notice stage is reported by only one source among those reviewed and is flagged here as a preliminary observation rather than a settled finding. The respondent's name was not given in any report reviewed and is therefore left unstated rather than guessed. No source reviewed gave the full text of the Supreme Court's order, so no direct quotation beyond the operative lines reported by LiveLaw is used.
